title: Inside or Outside the DRG: The Payment Window, APCs and the Lab Fee Schedule
summary: Learn why an inpatient test is a cost inside one DRG payment, which outpatient tests fall into the Medicare payment window before admission, and when hospital outpatient lab tests are packaged into outpatient payment or paid on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule.

reviewer.note: Teaches Ch. 13 Hits 1, 2 and 12 and Exam Trap 2. Checked against the eCFR text of 42 CFR 412.2, 412.60, 414.507, 414.510, 419.1, 419.2, 419.20, 419.21, 419.22 and 419.31 (version 2026-10-01), the CMS Three Day Payment Window and Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule pages and the CMS Medicare Claims Processing Manual chapter 16, section 30.3. The reviewer states the rule as a 72-hour window; the regulation counts the admission day plus the 3 calendar days before it (admission day plus 1 day before it for non-IPPS hospitals), and a lab test’s date of service is normally the collection date, not the order date (rv-payment-window-calendar-days). The reviewer’s Hit 12 says lab tests are generally still paid on the fee schedule; the regulation excludes them from OPPS except certain packaged tests, and the CMS Claims Processing Manual (ch. 16, 30.3) states that since 2014 an OPPS hospital’s outpatient lab tests are generally packaged, with separate CLFS payment when lab tests are the only outpatient service that day (rv-opps-lab-packaging). The cost-center/revenue-center wording is taught as the reviewer’s managerial framing of the payment rules. Not taught: the 14-day post-discharge rule and other Number Vault figures, capitation, leases, budgeting, the CLIA competency schedule. US Medicare rules only; Philippine and PhilHealth rules are not covered.

objectives: Explain why an inpatient laboratory test adds cost but not payment under a per-discharge DRG payment.
Apply the Medicare payment window: which hospital outpatient tests before an admission go on the inpatient claim.
State when a hospital outpatient’s clinical laboratory tests are packaged into OPPS payment and when they are paid on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule.

scenes.title: Monday draw, Thursday admission
scenes.altText: Invented scenario: a Medicare patient has a basic metabolic panel and CBC drawn at the hospital’s own outpatient laboratory on Monday morning and is admitted as an inpatient to the same acute-care (IPPS) hospital on Thursday evening, more than 72 hours later. A second set of tests was collected on Wednesday by an independent reference laboratory that the hospital does not own or operate. The billing clerk plans to send both as separate outpatient claims. Question token: “Inpatient claim, or bill separately?”

cues.text: A Medicare patient has blood drawn at the hospital’s own outpatient lab on Monday morning, and is admitted to the same hospital on Thursday evening, more than seventy-two hours later.
Another set of tests was collected on Wednesday by an independent reference lab that the hospital neither owns nor operates. The clerk plans separate outpatient claims for both.
Which tests go on the inpatient claim, and which are billed separately?

scenes.title: Two ways Medicare pays for a test
scenes.altText: Two doors. INPATIENT door (42 CFR 412.2 and 412.60): under the inpatient prospective payment system the hospital receives a predetermined amount per discharge; that payment covers inpatient operating costs, explicitly including ancillary services such as laboratory services; each discharge is assigned to one DRG (diagnosis-related group) regardless of the number of services furnished, and each DRG has a weighting factor reflecting its relative resource cost. So an extra inpatient test generally adds cost but not payment (an additional outlier payment is made for extraordinarily costly cases, 412.2(a)); the CMS Claims Processing Manual (ch. 16, 30.3) states that lab tests for a Part A inpatient are included in the PPS rate. PER-TEST door (42 CFR 414.507; CMS Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule page; Claims Processing Manual ch. 16, 30.3): a separately paid clinical diagnostic laboratory test is paid from the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule; since 2018 the rate for most tests is based on the weighted median of private payor rates.

cues.text: Medicare pays for an inpatient stay with one predetermined amount per discharge, under the inpatient prospective payment system.
That amount covers the hospital’s operating costs, including laboratory services, and each stay is assigned to a single diagnosis-related group, no matter how many services were given.

So for an inpatient, an extra test generally adds cost to the hospital but no extra payment, apart from extra outlier payments for extraordinarily costly cases. The lab works as a cost inside a fixed price.

A lab test that is paid on its own is different. It is paid per test from the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule, and since 2018 the rate for most tests is based on the weighted median of private payer rates.

props.label: One DRG per stay, any number of tests
Extra inpatient test = cost, not revenue

scenes.title: The payment window
scenes.altText: Window card (42 CFR 412.2(c)(5); CMS Three Day Payment Window page): for a subsection (d) hospital paid under IPPS, outpatient services furnished on the date of admission and during the 3 calendar days immediately preceding it are treated as inpatient operating costs and go on the Part A inpatient claim. Who card: only services furnished by the hospital or by an entity wholly owned (hospital is sole owner) or wholly operated (hospital has exclusive responsibility for routine operations) by it. What card: all diagnostic services, including clinical diagnostic laboratory tests, are included; nondiagnostic services only if related to the admission (since June 25, 2010, the hospital may attest that they are unrelated). One-day card: for non-subsection (d) hospitals (psychiatric, rehabilitation, long-term care, children’s and cancer hospitals) the window is the admission date plus 1 day before it. Date card: the date of service of a lab test is generally the date the specimen was collected (42 CFR 414.510(a)).

cues.text: Here is the rule. For an acute-care hospital paid under the inpatient system, outpatient services on the day of admission and on the three calendar days before it can belong on the inpatient claim.
It covers only services furnished by the hospital itself, or by an entity the hospital wholly owns or wholly operates.
Diagnostic services, including clinical lab tests, are always included. Nondiagnostic services are included only if they relate to the admission.

Psychiatric, rehabilitation, long-term care, children’s and cancer hospitals count only one day before admission instead. And for a lab test, the date of service is normally the day the specimen was collected, not the day it was ordered.

props.title: Admission day + 3 calendar days
lines: Goes on the Part A claim

props.label: Hospital or entity it wholly owns/operates
Lab date of service = specimen collection date

scenes.title: Outpatient side: APCs and the fee schedule
scenes.altText: OPPS card (42 CFR 419.1, 419.20, 419.31): the hospital outpatient prospective payment system took effect for services furnished from July 1, 2000 (applicability to hospitals stated as August 1, 2000); services that are clinically comparable and similar in resource use are grouped into Ambulatory Payment Classification (APC) groups, each with a payment weight. Exclusion card (419.22(l), 419.2(b)(17)): clinical diagnostic laboratory tests are excluded from OPPS payment, except certain tests whose payment is packaged into the related outpatient procedure or service. Practice token (CMS Claims Processing Manual ch. 16, 30.3): for OPPS hospitals, since January 1, 2014 outpatient lab tests are generally packaged as ancillary services; they are paid separately on the CLFS when the hospital provides only outpatient lab tests to the patient that day. Critical access hospitals are excluded from OPPS (419.20(b)(2)). Hook answer card: Monday’s hospital tests fall in the window (Wednesday, Tuesday and Monday are the 3 calendar days before a Thursday admission) and go on the inpatient claim even though more than 72 hours passed; Wednesday’s independent-lab tests are outside the window rule.

cues.text: For hospital outpatients, Medicare introduced its outpatient prospective payment system in 2000. It groups services that are clinically similar and cost about the same into Ambulatory Payment Classifications, or APCs.
The regulation carves clinical lab tests out of that system, except certain tests that are packaged, meaning their payment is folded into the payment for a related outpatient service.

And CMS’s manual says that since 2014, a hospital outpatient’s lab tests are generally packaged. They are paid separately on the lab fee schedule when lab tests are the only outpatient service that day.

Back to the hook. Wednesday, Tuesday and Monday are the three calendar days before a Thursday admission, so Monday’s hospital tests go on the inpatient claim, even after more than seventy-two hours. The independent lab’s Wednesday tests are not covered by the window rule.

props.label: Lab-only visit → paid on the CLFS

props.title: Hook answer
lines: Wed independent lab → outside the window

scenes.title: Three classic traps
scenes.altText: Three trap cards: “The order arrived 2 days before admission, so bill it as outpatient” (✓ hospital diagnostic tests in the window go on the inpatient claim; what counts is the date of service, normally the collection date); “It is a 72-hour clock” (✓ it is the admission day plus 3 calendar days before, or 1 day for non-IPPS hospitals); “Hospital outpatient lab tests are always paid per test on the fee schedule” (✓ at an OPPS hospital they are usually packaged with the other outpatient services that day; they are paid on the CLFS when lab tests are the only outpatient service).

cues.text: Trap one: the order came in two days before admission, so bill it as outpatient. No: a diagnostic test the hospital performed in the window goes on the inpatient claim.
Trap two: it is a seventy-two-hour clock. No: count calendar days, the admission day plus the three days before it, or one day before it for hospitals not paid under the inpatient system.

Trap three: hospital outpatient lab tests are always paid per test on the fee schedule. No: they are usually packaged with the other outpatient services that day, and paid on the fee schedule when they are the only service.

props.title: ✗ “Ordered 2 days before, bill as outpatient.”
lines: ✓ Hospital diagnostic test in window → inpatient claim

scenes.title: Three days back, same owner
scenes.altText: Memory aid: “Three days back, same owner: count the admission day and three calendar days back, and bundle only what the hospital’s own lab (or a lab it wholly owns or operates) did.” Tokens: Admission day + 3 calendar days · Same owner/operator · Inpatient = one DRG. A card lists where the aid breaks.

cues.text: Memory aid: three days back, same owner. Count the admission day and three calendar days back, and bundle only what the hospital, or a lab it wholly owns or operates, performed.

Where it breaks: hospitals not paid under the inpatient system count one day before admission; nondiagnostic services count only if related to the admission; ownership or operation decides, not the building; and these are US Medicare rules only.

props.title: Where it breaks

scenes.title: Takeaway
scenes.altText: Two tokens: “Inpatient = one DRG payment per stay; diagnostic tests by the hospital (or its wholly owned/operated entity) on the admission day + 3 calendar days before → inpatient claim”, “Hospital outpatient lab tests = usually packaged; lab-only visit = Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule”.

cues.text: Medicare pays an acute-care hospital one DRG amount per inpatient stay, so diagnostic tests that the hospital or an entity it wholly owns or operates furnishes on the admission day or the three calendar days before go on the inpatient claim, while a hospital outpatient’s lab tests are usually packaged with the other outpatient services that day and are paid per test on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule when they are the only service.

props.label: One DRG per stay · admission day + 3 calendar days · same owner
Outpatient lab: usually packaged; lab-only visit = CLFS

explanation.what: Plain language: for a hospital stay, Medicare pays one set price, so the hospital’s tests during the stay, and the hospital’s diagnostic tests in the few days just before it, are covered by that one price. A hospital outpatient’s lab tests are usually folded into the payment for the other outpatient services that day; when they are paid on their own, they are paid test by test from a price list. Scientific terms: inpatient prospective payment system (IPPS), payment per discharge, diagnosis-related group (DRG) and weighting factor, subsection (d) hospital, 3-day (or 1-day) payment window, wholly owned or operated entity, diagnostic vs nondiagnostic services, date of service, hospital outpatient prospective payment system (OPPS), Ambulatory Payment Classification (APC), packaging, Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule (CLFS).
explanation.why: The DRG payment is predetermined and covers ancillary services such as laboratory work, and a discharge gets one DRG regardless of how many services were furnished, so inpatient testing is a cost to manage. The law defines inpatient operating costs to include the hospital’s diagnostic services shortly before admission, so those charges belong on the inpatient (Part A) claim rather than on separate outpatient claims.
explanation.measure: Window: admission day + 3 calendar days before (subsection (d) IPPS hospitals); admission day + 1 day before for psychiatric, rehabilitation, long-term care, children’s and cancer hospitals. Covered: services by the hospital or an entity it wholly owns (sole owner) or wholly operates (exclusive responsibility for routine operations). Diagnostic services (including clinical lab tests) always; nondiagnostic only if related (since June 25, 2010). Lab date of service: normally the specimen collection date. OPPS: services from July 1, 2000; APCs group clinically comparable services with similar resource use; clinical lab tests excluded except certain packaged tests; per the CMS Claims Processing Manual, since January 1, 2014 an OPPS hospital’s outpatient lab tests are generally packaged, and are paid separately on the CLFS when the hospital provides only outpatient lab tests that day. CLFS rates since 2018: for most tests, based on the weighted median of private payor rates.
explanation.differs: Calendar-day window vs a 72-hour clock; collection date vs order date; hospital-owned or operated laboratory vs independent laboratory; diagnostic vs nondiagnostic services; IPPS (3-day) vs non-IPPS (1-day) hospitals; packaged payment (lab tests with other outpatient services) vs separate fee-schedule payment (lab-only visit).
explanation.examAngle: Expect: decide whether a pre-admission test is billed on the inpatient claim, identify the exception for an independent laboratory, or say whether a hospital outpatient’s laboratory tests are packaged or paid on the fee schedule.

takeaway: Medicare pays an acute-care hospital one DRG amount per inpatient stay, so diagnostic tests that the hospital or an entity it wholly owns or operates furnishes on the admission day or the three calendar days before go on the inpatient claim, while a hospital outpatient’s lab tests are usually packaged with the other outpatient services that day and are paid per test on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule when they are the only service.

questions.stem: A Medicare patient’s blood is collected at an acute-care (IPPS) hospital’s outpatient laboratory at 8 a.m. on Monday for a diagnostic panel. The patient is admitted as an inpatient to the same hospital at 6 p.m. on Thursday. How should the Monday test be billed?

options.text: On the inpatient (Part A) claim for the stay
options.rationale: Correct. Monday is one of the 3 calendar days before a Thursday admission, and diagnostic services furnished by the hospital in that window are included on the inpatient claim.

options.text: As a separate outpatient claim, because more than 72 hours passed
options.rationale: Incorrect. The window counts calendar days (admission day plus the 3 days before), not hours.

options.text: As a separate outpatient claim, because it was ordered before the admission decision
options.rationale: Incorrect. Diagnostic services in the window are included regardless of when they were ordered; the lab date of service is normally the collection date.

options.text: Only after the patient signs an Advance Beneficiary Notice
options.rationale: Incorrect. The payment-window conditions in 42 CFR 412.2(c)(5) are who furnished the service, what kind of service it is and when it was furnished; they include no beneficiary-notice condition.

questions.stem: Two days before an inpatient admission to an IPPS hospital, which of these laboratory services would NOT be included on the hospital’s inpatient claim under the payment window?

options.text: Tests performed by an independent laboratory that the hospital neither owns nor operates
options.rationale: Correct. The window applies only to services furnished by the hospital or by an entity it wholly owns or wholly operates.

options.text: Tests performed in the hospital’s own outpatient laboratory
options.rationale: Incorrect. Hospital-furnished diagnostic tests in the window go on the inpatient claim.

options.text: Tests performed by an off-site laboratory of which the hospital is the sole owner
options.rationale: Incorrect. Services of an entity the hospital wholly owns (it is the sole owner) fall under the rule; the regulation sets no location condition.

options.text: Tests performed by the hospital that seem unrelated to the reason for admission
options.rationale: Incorrect. Diagnostic services, including clinical lab tests, are included whether or not they relate to the admission; only nondiagnostic services can be attested as unrelated.

questions.stem: A Medicare patient comes to a hospital paid under the outpatient prospective payment system (OPPS) only for a blood draw and two chemistry tests, and receives no other hospital outpatient service that day. According to the CMS Claims Processing Manual, how are the tests paid?

options.text: Separately, per test, on the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule
options.rationale: Correct. For OPPS hospitals, outpatient lab tests are eligible for separate CLFS payment when the hospital provides only outpatient lab tests to the patient that day (Claims Processing Manual ch. 16, 30.3).

options.text: Packaged into the OPPS payment for a related outpatient service
options.rationale: Incorrect. Since 2014 lab tests are generally packaged when they come with other hospital outpatient services, but here there is no other service to package them into.

options.text: Through the DRG for the patient’s diagnosis
options.rationale: Incorrect. DRGs classify inpatient discharges (42 CFR 412.60), and this patient was not admitted.

options.text: Through a fixed payment per member per month
options.rationale: Incorrect. Medicare sets a payment rate for each clinical diagnostic laboratory test (42 CFR 414.507), not a fixed monthly amount per enrollee.

accuracyFlags.issue: The reviewer (Hit 1, Trap 2, Number Vault, figure caption, Memory Hook) states a 72-hour window tied to when tests were ordered. 42 CFR 412.2(c)(5) and the CMS payment-window page count the admission date plus the 3 calendar days before it (1 day before it for non-subsection (d) hospitals), limited to services furnished by the hospital or an entity it wholly owns or operates, and 42 CFR 414.510 sets a lab test’s date of service as the collection date. A test collected more than 72 hours before admission can still fall in the window. The lesson teaches the regulation.

The reviewer’s Hit 12 says clinical lab tests are generally still paid on the fee schedule. 42 CFR 419.22(l) excludes them from OPPS except as provided in 419.2(b)(17), which packages certain clinical diagnostic laboratory tests into the payment for the related service, and the CMS Claims Processing Manual (ch. 16, 30.3) states that since January 1, 2014 an OPPS hospital’s outpatient lab tests are generally packaged, with separate CLFS payment when lab tests are the only outpatient service that day. The fee-schedule statement holds for those lab-only visits, not as the general rule for hospital outpatients. The lesson teaches the packaging rule.

DRG/IPPS, the payment window, OPPS/APCs and the Clinical Laboratory Fee Schedule are US Medicare rules. Philippine and PhilHealth payment rules are not covered (see register flag rv-us-centric); MTLE candidates should check local requirements.
